paragraphs: An image classifier can change its prediction when its input receives a carefully constructed modification that a person barely notices. Studying these adversarial examples helps expose vulnerabilities in learned classifiers. This paper introduces AdvFlow, a black-box attack method designed to produce such examples while making them resemble ordinary image data.

The approach uses normalizing flows to model the density of adversarial examples around a particular target image. This makes the distribution of generated examples central to the attack: the method aims to produce misleading inputs that also follow the distribution of clean data. The authors observe this resemblance and connect it to a lower likelihood of detection.

Experiments report competitive performance against some existing attack methods on defended classifiers. That finding supports AdvFlow as a useful attack approach in the evaluated settings, while its distributional behavior highlights an additional concern for defenses. An adversarial input may be difficult to identify not only because its visual changes are subtle, but also because it resembles the data a classifier normally encounters.
neurips-2020-advflow-inconspicuous-black.tldr: AdvFlow uses normalizing flows to generate black-box adversarial images that resemble clean data and perform competitively against some attacks on defended classifiers.

paragraphs: Many approaches to adversarial learning assume that test inputs are small modifications of ordinary examples. This paper considers a broader setting: training examples come from a distribution P, while the unlabeled test examples can be arbitrary. The learner receives those test inputs in advance, making the problem transductive rather than requiring predictions for unseen future inputs.

The algorithm produces a selective classifier, which can decline to predict on some examples. This option enables guarantees for function classes with bounded VC dimension, a measure of their expressive capacity. The guarantees combine low test error with a low rejection rate measured against P. The reference distribution matters: the rejection guarantee does not say that few arbitrary adversarial inputs must be accepted or rejected.

The algorithm is efficient when an empirical risk minimizer for the function class is available. Its guarantees cover even an adversary with unlimited computation and full knowledge of the learner. The paper also establishes results for generalization, agnostic learning, and unsupervised settings, extending the role of selective prediction beyond small-perturbation robustness.
neurips-2020-beyond-perturbations-learni.tldr: Selective transductive learning provides guarantees for arbitrary adversarial test inputs by allowing abstention while keeping rejection low on the training distribution.

paragraphs: An AI agent often optimizes a reward function intended to represent what its user wants. That representation can omit parts of the user's preferences. This paper studies the consequences through a mathematical model of a principal and an agent operating with constrained resources, where multiple features of the world contribute to the principal's overall utility.

The model explicitly assumes that the agent's reward depends on only J of the L relevant features, with J smaller than L. Within this setup, the authors give necessary and sufficient conditions under which indefinitely optimizing any incomplete proxy drives overall utility arbitrarily low. The result is conditional on those conditions; it does not establish that every incomplete reward inevitably produces that outcome.

The paper also examines changes that can produce higher-utility solutions. These include allowing rewards to reference the full state and letting the principal revise the proxy over time. The analysis therefore gives a theoretical reason to treat reward design as an ongoing interaction: updating an objective can matter when its initial specification leaves out things the user values.
neurips-2020-consequences-of-misaligned-.tldr: A resource-constrained principal–agent model identifies when optimizing incomplete rewards can drive utility arbitrarily low and how interactive reward updates can help.

paragraphs: Continual learning studies how a model learns from changing data while retaining useful previous knowledge. Many evaluation settings organize that data into distinct tasks. This paper instead targets General Continual Learning, where task boundaries are unclear, distributions can change gradually or abruptly, and collecting data for offline training is not a viable option.

The proposed baseline, Dark Experience Replay, combines rehearsal, knowledge distillation, and regularization. Its central mechanism matches the network's logits, or prediction scores, recorded at different points during training. Reusing these past outputs encourages the current network to remain consistent with earlier versions of itself. Historical predictions thus become a learning signal alongside experience from the changing stream.

The authors evaluate the method on standard benchmarks and a new setting called MNIST-360. They report that this simple combination outperforms established approaches while using limited resources. They also investigate generalization and find benefits from the regularization beyond the main performance comparison. The results make consistency with past predictions a strong baseline for learning under blurred task boundaries.
neurips-2020-dark-experience-for-general.tldr: Dark Experience Replay improves continual learning by rehearsing experience and matching past prediction scores as data distributions change.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning seeks a posterior distribution over model parameters rather than only a single fitted solution. This paper develops a collaborative algorithm in which multiple agents perform that learning through decentralized Langevin dynamics. The analysis addresses a non-convex setting and asks how the resulting Markov chain approaches the desired posterior.

The authors measure distributional error using KL divergence and distinguish contributions with different rates of decay. The contribution from the initial discrepancy decreases exponentially, while contributions associated with additive noise decrease polynomially. They further show that the polynomial term improves with the number of agents. These separate terms explain why the overall convergence behavior cannot be described by one exponential rate.

The theory supplies sufficient conditions on changing step sizes that guarantee convergence to the target distribution. Across the evaluated machine learning tasks, individual agents using locally available data achieve performance comparable to a centralized setup, with substantially improved convergence rates. Together, the analysis and experiments support decentralized collaboration as a way to perform Bayesian learning while distributing access to training data.
neurips-2020-decentralized-langevin-dyna.tldr: Decentralized Langevin dynamics enables collaborative Bayesian learning, with convergence guarantees under step-size conditions and empirical performance comparable to centralized learning.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation depends on expert annotations, but experts can disagree because of differing biases and competence. Treating every annotation as exact ground truth can therefore restrict what a model learns. This paper aims to separate the underlying segmentation label distribution from the errors introduced by individual annotators, using only noisy observations.

The method couples two convolutional neural networks to learn segmentation and annotator reliability jointly. Its separation principle is unusual: it encourages the estimated annotators to be as unreliable as possible while still explaining the observed training labels accurately. This objective provides a way to distinguish the inferred segmentation from the process that produced imperfect annotations.

The authors first study the algorithm on a segmentation dataset built from MNIST, then evaluate it on medical datasets covering multiple-sclerosis lesions, brain tumors, and lung abnormalities. The experiments use real annotations and simulated ones where necessary. The method outperforms the compared approaches, especially with few annotations and substantial disagreement, and captures complex spatial patterns in annotators' mistakes.
neurips-2020-disentangling-human-error-f.tldr: Two coupled networks jointly infer medical image segmentations and annotator errors from noisy labels, improving results especially when annotations are scarce and disagree.

paragraphs: Success in fixed-team, zero-sum games does not fully address situations where agents must decide when to cooperate and when to compete. Social dilemmas are particularly challenging because individually selfish behavior can undermine collective outcomes. This paper investigates whether broadening agents' training experiences can encourage more flexible social behavior.

The proposed augmentation, randomized uncertain social preferences, or RUSP, expands the distribution of environments that agents encounter during training. The authors describe it as generic and scalable, applicable to multi-agent environments without altering their underlying game dynamics or original objectives. Its purpose is to create training conditions in which socially responsive strategies can emerge.

The experiments provide evidence of direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity and reputation, and team formation. These behaviors can lead to equilibria with higher social welfare in the tested settings, which include the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and more complex environments with consequences unfolding over time. The contribution is evidence that the training distribution can support these behaviors, rather than a guarantee that every trained agent will cooperate.
neurips-2020-emergent-reciprocity-and-te.tldr: Randomized uncertain social preferences can produce reciprocity, reputation, and team formation in trained agents, supporting higher social welfare in tested dilemmas.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a decision-making policy from expert demonstrations. Although many methods have been evaluated experimentally, understanding their errors theoretically remains important. This paper compares behavioral cloning and generative adversarial imitation by analyzing the gap in value between an expert policy and the policy learned by imitation.

The bounds support the conclusion that adversarial imitation can reduce the accumulation of errors compared with behavioral cloning. Errors matter across a sequence of decisions because their effects can compound, so reducing that accumulation also improves the sample complexity described by the analysis. The comparison connects the learning method to the amount of demonstration data needed for performance.

The paper then extends this reasoning to learning an environment's transition model. By treating the environment as a dual agent, its behavior can also be viewed as something to imitate. Applying the policy bounds to this perspective suggests that adversarial imitation can learn environment models more effectively than behavioral cloning. This creates a theoretical motivation for using adversarial imitation within model-based reinforcement learning.
neurips-2020-error-bounds-of-imitating-p.tldr: Error bounds support adversarial imitation over behavioral cloning for reducing compounding policy errors and for learning environment models.

paragraphs: Few-shot image generation asks a model to create images in a domain represented by only a handful of training examples. Those examples cannot reasonably reveal the domain's entire distribution. This paper therefore starts with a model pretrained on a larger, related source domain and adapts it to the target domain.

The objective is to combine the source model's diversity with the target examples' appearance. Adaptation changes the existing model without adding parameters. Crucially, the method regularizes weight changes so that fitting the new examples also preserves information acquired from the source dataset. This makes retaining prior knowledge an explicit part of the adaptation process.

The authors demonstrate high-quality generation across different target domains, including cases with only ten examples. They also examine how performance depends on the number of target examples and the similarity between source and target domains. The results support constrained adaptation as a way to use a rich source model when the target data alone provide little information about possible visual variation.
neurips-2020-few-shot-image-generation-w.tldr: Regularizing changes to a pretrained image generator enables adaptation from very few target examples while aiming to preserve source-domain diversity.

paragraphs: Suppose only k of n uncertain candidates can be considered, and success depends on the highest or second-highest value among those selected. This paper studies that selection problem when each random variable has an explicit description. One application is a second-price auction, where participation constraints affect both the winning bid and the payment.

The two objectives have sharply different computational properties. For the expected highest value, the authors give a polynomial-time approximation scheme, allowing increasingly accurate approximation for a fixed accuracy choice. For the expected second-highest value, they show that no polynomial-time constant-factor approximation exists assuming the Planted Clique Hypothesis. That hardness conclusion depends on the stated hypothesis.

A distributional assumption changes the picture. If every random variable has monotone hazard rate, selecting the k variables with the largest upper-tail quantile values at probability 1 divided by the square root of k gives a constant-factor approximation to both objectives simultaneously. Thus, a simple scoring rule becomes provably useful under this assumption, despite the broader difficulty of optimizing the second-highest value.
neurips-2020-hitting-the-high-notes-subs.tldr: Selecting for the expected maximum is approximable, the second maximum is conditionally hard, and a simple quantile rule approximates both under monotone hazard rates.

paragraphs: Quantum-inspired embedding represents a knowledge base using vectors intended to preserve its logical structure. The earlier approach is described as supporting Boolean-style deductive reasoning over those vectors for hierarchies of unary and binary predicates. However, its original formulation is transductive, and training is slow for applications involving millions of entities.

This paper reformulates the embedding problem to support induction, extending the approach beyond its original transductive setting. During that reformulation, the authors identify analytic and geometric properties of the solution. They use those properties to develop a faster training scheme, addressing both the scope of the representation and the practical cost of learning it.

The application is fine-grained entity type classification, a language-processing task that assigns detailed types to entities. The inductive approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the reported task, and its training runs nine times faster than the original quantum embedding scheme there. These findings show that changing the formulation can make the embedding approach more useful while substantially reducing training time in the evaluated application.
neurips-2020-inductive-quantum-embedding.tldr: An inductive reformulation of quantum-inspired knowledge embeddings achieves strong entity typing results and trains nine times faster than the original scheme on that task.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernels are used to model how heavily overparameterized neural networks train, but their generalization can lag behind that of practical networks. This paper attributes part of the gap to their lack of label awareness. In the authors' account, ignoring labels also makes these kernels less locally elastic than the networks they aim to represent.

The authors propose two kernels that explicitly incorporate label information. Each combines a label-independent component with a hierarchy of label-dependent components. The hierarchy uses the Hoeffding decomposition, organizing the additional components by increasingly complex dependence on labels. This gives a structured way to add label sensitivity to the kernel.

The paper supplies both theoretical and empirical evidence that models using these kernels better reproduce neural networks' generalization and local elasticity. The claim is an improvement in the correspondence between kernel models and networks, with label awareness addressing one identified source of the gap. The contribution therefore concerns both predictive behavior and the usefulness of kernels as models of neural-network learning.
neurips-2020-label-aware-neural-tangent-.tldr: Two label-aware neural tangent kernels better reproduce neural networks' generalization and local elasticity through structured label-dependent components.

paragraphs: Reward shaping adds a learning signal that expresses domain knowledge to a reinforcement learning problem. Human knowledge can be translated imperfectly into numerical rewards, however, so fully following that signal may not improve the actual task. This paper asks how an agent can learn to use a supplied shaping reward selectively.

The approach formulates this choice as a two-level optimization problem. At the lower level, shaping rewards guide policy optimization. At the upper level, a parameterized weighting function is adjusted to maximize the true reward. The authors derive the gradient of expected true reward with respect to the weighting parameters and develop three algorithms under different assumptions.

Experiments use sparse-reward cartpole and MuJoCo environments. The reported results show that the algorithms can exploit helpful shaping rewards while ignoring unhelpful ones or even turning them into useful guidance. This makes the quality of shaping depend on its contribution to the true objective, allowing the learner to adapt how it uses domain knowledge rather than treating every supplied shaping value as equally helpful.
neurips-2020-learning-to-utilize-shaping.tldr: A two-level optimization learns how to weight shaping rewards according to their effect on true task reward.

paragraphs: Visual attention influences which parts of a scene receive stronger neural representation. A model predicting brain responses from visual input can therefore benefit from knowing where a person attends. This paper studies that connection using simultaneous eye-tracking and fMRI recordings from a large group of people watching movies.

The authors first incorporate measured gaze through attentional masking and find a significant improvement in brain-response prediction accuracy. They then introduce a trainable soft-attention module into the neural encoding model. This second approach learns end to end from fMRI responses alone, without requiring eye-tracking data to supervise the attention mechanism.

On independent data, the model's estimated attention locations agree well with the corresponding eye fixations, even though those fixations were not explicitly used as training targets. The finding suggests that learning to predict brain responses can also reveal informative patterns of visual attention. Together, the two approaches support attention as a useful component of neural encoding, whether attention is supplied through gaze measurements or learned from brain-response data.
neurips-2020-neural-encoding-with-visual.tldr: Attention improves visual brain-response modeling, and an attention module trained only on fMRI learns locations that agree with independently measured eye fixations.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates the range and likelihood of future returns, rather than only their average. Quantiles offer one way to represent that distribution, but their values should increase as the quantile level increases. Batch-based learning can violate this ordering, especially early in training, producing abnormal and less interpretable distribution estimates.

The paper introduces a framework based on non-crossing quantile regression. It enforces the required ordering within each sampled batch and is designed to integrate with existing distributional reinforcement learning algorithms. The authors support the method through both theoretical analysis and implementation, connecting a basic distributional constraint to a practical training modification.

On Atari 2600 games, some leading algorithms equipped with the modification converge faster and achieve better test performance than their baselines. The authors also report that recovering distribution information can substantially improve exploration when rewards are extremely sparse. The findings link coherent quantile estimates to useful learning behavior, with the empirical improvements established for the evaluated algorithms and environments.
neurips-2020-non-crossing-quantile-regre.tldr: Enforcing non-crossing quantiles within training batches improves return-distribution estimates and can accelerate learning and exploration in distributional reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks aim to express uncertainty through a predictive distribution, but computing that distribution usually requires approximation. This paper investigates how two common approximations, mean-field Gaussian distributions and Monte Carlo dropout, constrain the uncertainty that a network can represent. The distinction between limitations of the model and of inference is central.

For ReLU networks with one hidden layer, the authors prove that simple cases exist where neither approximation can substantially raise uncertainty between separated regions of low uncertainty. Strong empirical evidence indicates that exact inference avoids this pathology. That comparison points to the approximation as the source of the problem, rather than to an inherent inability of the Bayesian network.

For deeper networks, the paper proves that approximate posteriors in these same families exist that can express flexible uncertainty. Yet experiments show that variational inference can still produce similar pathological behavior. The results distinguish representational possibility from the outcome of fitting: a sufficiently expressive approximation family does not by itself ensure that training finds a satisfactory uncertainty estimate.
neurips-2020-on-the-expressiveness-of-ap.tldr: Common Bayesian neural-network approximations restrict shallow-network uncertainty, while deeper networks can express flexible uncertainty that variational training may still fail to recover.

paragraphs: Some neural networks become effectively linear in their parameters as their width tends to infinity, even though their construction uses nonlinear components. This behavior is associated with a constant neural tangent kernel. The paper investigates what causes that transition and which aspects of network architecture determine whether it occurs.

The explanation centers on how the norm of the network's Hessian changes with width. The Hessian describes curvature with respect to parameters, so its scaling provides a way to understand the disappearance of nonlinear parameter dependence. The authors develop a general framework based on this relationship for standard network classes, offering a perspective distinct from the usual explanation through lazy training.

The analysis also establishes boundaries on the phenomenon. Increasing width does not make every network enter this linear regime; the transition fails when the last layer is nonlinear. Moreover, the transition is not necessary for gradient descent to optimize successfully. These findings separate network width, parameter-space linearity, and optimization success, showing why they should not automatically be treated as equivalent.
neurips-2020-on-the-linearity-of-large-n.tldr: Hessian scaling explains constant tangent kernels in certain wide networks, while showing that linearization is neither universal nor required for successful gradient descent.

paragraphs: Topological features describe structural properties of data that can be useful for learning. This paper introduces PLLay, a neural-network layer based on persistence landscapes, to make such information available within general deep learning models. The aim is to let later layers use topological structure as part of solving the task.

The authors show differentiability with respect to layer inputs for general persistent homology with arbitrary filtration. This supports placing PLLay at any position in a network and learning its task-specific structure through backpropagation. The approach does not require a separate input featurization or preprocessing stage, bringing the topological representation into the trainable model itself.

The paper also develops an adaptation using a distance-to-measure function-based filtration and provides a stability analysis supporting robustness to noise and outliers. Classification experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Together, these contributions address both integration and reliability: topological information can participate in end-to-end training, while the stability results explain resistance to disruptions in the data.
neurips-2020-pllay-efficient-topological.tldr: PLLay integrates trainable persistence-landscape features into neural networks, with differentiability and stability results supporting end-to-end use.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents must discover combinations of actions that work together, but the space of joint actions grows exponentially with the number of agents. Exploring independently is more manageable, yet can fail when success requires elaborate group strategies. This paper studies whether encouraging coordination in the policies themselves can guide exploration toward useful collective behavior.

The authors introduce two policy regularizers. TeamReg encourages predictability of actions between agents, while CoachReg encourages synchronized selection of behaviors. Both use a proposed proxy for coordination to bias learning. The idea is that these policy qualities can make coordinated exploration easier to discover, even when rewards provide limited guidance.

Evaluation covers four continuous-control tasks with sparse rewards and different coordination demands, plus the discrete-action Google Research Football environment. The experiments show performance improvements across many cooperative problems. Further analysis finds that the learned policies exhibit the predictability or synchronization targeted by the methods. This connects the observed gains with the intended behavioral changes, while keeping those changes framed as proxies for coordination.
neurips-2020-promoting-coordination-thro.tldr: TeamReg and CoachReg encourage action predictability and synchronized behavior selection, improving performance across many evaluated cooperative multi-agent tasks.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization evaluates a sequence of decisions through regret: the accumulated loss relative to a comparison decision. Standard regret guarantees commonly assume Lipschitz continuity, which controls how sharply losses change. Strong convexity can yield stronger guarantees. This paper asks how far those results extend when the classical assumptions are replaced by their relative versions.

Relative Lipschitz continuity and relative strong convexity generalize the corresponding classical conditions. Earlier convex optimization work had established analogous performance for subgradient methods under these broader notions. The authors bring this perspective to online learning and extend known regret bounds for follow-the-regularized-leader algorithms and a variant of online mirror descent.

Because these methods cover many online optimization algorithms, the analysis yields guarantees for a broad collection of procedures. The paper also extends its results to methods with additional regularization, including regularized dual averaging. The significance is a wider theoretical scope: useful regret bounds remain available under generalized regularity conditions, expanding the loss functions that existing algorithmic frameworks can handle.
neurips-2020-regret-bounds-without-lipsc.tldr: Classical online optimization regret bounds extend to relative Lipschitz and relative strongly convex losses across several general algorithmic frameworks.

paragraphs: Multi-voxel pattern analysis uses fMRI measurements to distinguish cognitive tasks. Its predictive performance depends on informative features and enough examples, yet fMRI datasets are often small, noisy, and high-dimensional. Combining information across collection sites presents an additional challenge: corresponding cognitive tasks must be represented in a way that supports transfer between datasets.

Shared Space Transfer Learning addresses this through two stages. It first extracts features common to subjects within each site, then maps those site-specific features into a shared space that is independent of the site. This functional alignment is intended to make information from multiple sites useful for improving task prediction at each site.

The method uses a scalable optimization procedure designed for high-dimensional data, including a single-iteration algorithm for extracting each site's common features. Experiments assess transfer across various cognitive tasks and report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art analysis techniques. The approach makes shared representation learning central to multi-site prediction, with the stated setting focused on functionally aligning datasets involving homogeneous cognitive tasks.
neurips-2020-shared-space-transfer-learn.tldr: Shared Space Transfer Learning aligns site-specific fMRI features in a common representation to improve cognitive-task prediction across sites.

paragraphs: Combining multiple predictive models can improve accuracy and stability, particularly when training data are limited. This paper focuses on how to design that combination for neural networks. It introduces a diversified ensemble layer that brings multiple networks together as individual modules within a common architecture.

The theoretical analysis shows that each constituent model corresponds to ensemble-layer weights optimized in different directions. This gives the proposed diversity a specific optimization-based interpretation. The layer is designed to fit into several common architecture families, including convolutional, recurrent, and graph convolutional networks, making the ensemble mechanism applicable to different forms of data.

Experiments cover public tabular, image, and text datasets. With weight sharing, the method produces notable improvements in accuracy and stability while adding negligible time and space overhead in the reported results. This combination matters because the practical benefit of an ensemble depends on its cost as well as its predictions. The findings support structured diversity and shared weights as a useful design for efficient neural-network ensembles.
neurips-2020-the-diversified-ensemble-ne.tldr: A diversified ensemble layer combines neural modules optimized in different directions, improving accuracy and stability with negligible reported overhead when weights are shared.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns smaller subnetworks that can train in isolation and match the performance of a full model. This paper investigates whether such subnetworks already exist inside pretrained BERT, a common starting point for language tasks. It also asks whether a subnetwork identified using one task remains useful for other tasks.

Across a range of downstream tasks, the authors find matching subnetworks with sparsity between 40% and 90%. These subnetworks are present at the pretrained initialization, before downstream training. That distinction matters: the result concerns a starting point that already contains pretraining knowledge, and differs from earlier language-model findings in which matching subnetworks emerged only after additional training.

Transfer depends strongly on the task used to identify the subnetwork. Those found through masked language modeling, BERT's pretraining task, transfer across the evaluated tasks, while those found through other tasks transfer only narrowly or not at all. The findings extend lottery-ticket observations to pretrained models and show that the selection objective matters for finding broadly reusable sparse subnetworks.
neurips-2020-the-lottery-ticket-hypothes.tldr: Pretrained BERT contains matching subnetworks at 40–90% sparsity, with masked-language-modeling subnetworks transferring broadly across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: A graph neural network trained on one scale of graph may struggle when graph size, diameter, or edge weights change. This paper approaches that problem by borrowing structural ideas from graph algorithms. The authors aim to make learned computation behave more like an algorithm whose operation adapts to the graph being processed.

The first extension learns when to stop message passing according to computational progress, rather than relying on a fixed number of iterations. The second introduces homogeneous transformation layers, motivated by the consistent way many graph algorithms respond to rescaling weights. These layers can universally approximate homogeneous functions and are used to make otherwise ordinary graph neural networks homogeneous.

Experiments show that the resulting networks can learn from small graphs and generalize well to larger ones on several basic graph-theory problems. The authors also report generalization in multi-body physical simulation and image-based navigation. The results support adaptive computation and weight homogeneity as useful architectural choices for scale transfer, with evidence spanning both graph problems and additional applications.
neurips-2020-towards-scale-invariant-gra.tldr: Adaptive message-passing termination and homogeneous layers help graph neural networks trained on small graphs generalize to larger-scale problems.

paragraphs: Bayesian unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from a model's posterior beliefs. This paper studies approximate removal of a small subset of data. Its reference target is the exact posterior that would result from retraining on the remaining data, and it measures the discrepancy using KL divergence.

Within variational inference, the authors show that this objective is equivalent to minimizing an evidence upper bound. The bound balances removing information associated with erased data against retaining the posterior learned from the full dataset. Retention matters because that posterior also contains information from examples that should remain; excessive forgetting can make the model unusable.

A further difficulty is that variational training supplies only an approximate full-data posterior to begin with. The authors propose two techniques to address this complication and demonstrate their methods on sparse Gaussian process and logistic regression models using synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution is a principled objective for approximate unlearning that explicitly balances deletion with preservation of useful remaining knowledge.
neurips-2020-variational-bayesian-unlear.tldr: Variational Bayesian unlearning balances removing selected data's influence with retaining useful posterior knowledge, targeting the posterior from retraining on remaining data.
